passage: At the community centre's after-school club, Sabina was fitting the last blue sky pieces into a jigsaw when Bhupen Uncle called, "Sabina, your dance class is starting!" Twelve pieces were left. All through dance, she kept missing her steps, thinking about the gap in the corner where the sun should be. The moment class ended, she ran back down the corridor, ghungroo still jingling on her ankles, and snapped the pieces in one by one. "Done!" Bhupen Uncle held up a painting. "You finished this yesterday. Taking it home?" Sabina stared at it. "Oh. I forgot I made that."

qa.q: How many jigsaw pieces were left when Sabina was called away?
qa.a: Twelve pieces were left.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel during dance class, and why?
qa.a: She felt restless and distracted, because she kept thinking about the gap in the corner where the sun should be, so she missed her steps.

qa.q: What could Sabina try next time she has to leave a puzzle half done?
qa.a: Before leaving, she could say out loud where she will start again, like "the sun corner", so the puzzle feels parked and she can enjoy the dance.

qa.q: How might Bhupen Uncle see Sabina rushing back in her ghungroo?
qa.a: He may find it funny and a little surprising that she remembers twelve jigsaw pieces so clearly but has completely forgotten the painting she finished yesterday. 😄

grounding: A girl called away mid-jigsaw keeps thinking about it and rushes back to finish, while a painting she already finished slips from her mind.

passage: Kalyani here, Arnab's older sister. Last Sunday Arnab was doing the children's crossword in the newspaper when Ma sent him to the market for coriander. Two clues were still empty. He went, but he came back running, with the coriander squashed in his fist, and grabbed the pencil before he even took off his chappals. "Seven letters, a kind of boat!" he said to nobody. I asked him about the maths homework he had finished that morning, and he couldn't remember which chapter it was. I don't know what goes on in his head. But I noticed that the crossword seemed to stick to him, and the finished homework didn't.

qa.q: What did Ma send Arnab to the market for?
qa.a: Coriander.

qa.q: How can you tell the unfinished crossword stayed on Arnab's mind at the market?
qa.a: He came back running with the coriander squashed in his fist and grabbed the pencil before taking off his chappals, clearly still thinking about the two empty clues.

qa.q: How could Ma make the errand easier for Arnab next time?
qa.a: She could let him finish the last two clues first, or agree on when he'll come back to it, since an open puzzle clearly pulls at him.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see the difference between the crossword and the homework?
qa.a: Kalyani notices the unfinished crossword sticks to Arnab while the finished homework slips away, though she admits she can't know what is in his head.

grounding: A sister notices that her brother's half-done crossword stays on his mind while homework he already finished is quickly forgotten.

passage:
Friday: Chinmay was two turns away from finishing one face of his colour cube when his mother called him for dinner. He ate with one hand under the table, twisting an imaginary cube.
Saturday: At cricket practice he kept losing count of balls. His cousin Eshaan laughed, "Are you bowling with your eyes closed?" Chinmay didn't even hear. He was thinking about the corner piece. The minute he got home, he dropped his bat and grabbed the cube from the sofa.
Monday: Eshaan asked, "So, did you finish it?" Chinmay blinked. "Oh. Yes, yesterday." He couldn't remember which colour he had done first, or where he had put the cube. All he wanted to talk about was his new half-built paper tower.

qa.q: What was Chinmay doing when his mother called him for dinner?
qa.a: He was two turns away from finishing one face of his colour cube.

qa.q: What was Chinmay thinking about at cricket practice?
qa.a: He was thinking about the corner piece. The unfinished cube pulled at him so much that he lost count of balls and didn't hear Eshaan.

qa.q: What could Chinmay have done on Friday night so the cube bothered him less at practice?
qa.a: He could have asked for two more minutes to finish the face, or noted exactly where he stopped, so the task felt either closed or safely parked.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel when Chinmay doesn't react to the joke?
qa.a: Eshaan may feel a bit ignored or puzzled, since the joke gets no reaction while Chinmay's mind is still on the cube.

grounding: Across a few days, a boy's unfinished cube keeps nagging him until he completes it, after which it slips from memory and a new unfinished task takes over.

passage: Kamal, you left your crossword half done and now you can't sleep? Ha. Your Rukmini Paati knows that feeling. When I was nine, my father brought me a wooden tangram set from Madras. Seven pieces, and a card with a swan to make. I had the neck and the body, only the tail left, when Amma called me to fetch water from the well. All the way there and back, pot on my hip, I was turning triangles in my head. I spilled half the water hurrying. The moment I put the pot down, I ran to the veranda and fitted the last piece. A swan! That same morning I'd drawn a big kolam at the door. When Amma praised it that evening, I couldn't even remember what pattern I'd made. Finished things fly away, kanna. Unfinished ones sit on your shoulder.

qa.q: What shape was young Rukmini making with the tangram?
qa.a: She was making a swan, with only the tail left.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel while she fetched water?
qa.a: She felt restless and impatient to finish the swan's tail, turning triangles in her head so much that she spilled half the water hurrying.

qa.q: What could Kamal do if the half-done crossword keeps Kamal awake?
qa.a: Kamal could jot down where the crossword stopped or finish one clue before bed, so the open task stops tugging.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when Rukmini couldn't remember her own kolam?
qa.a: Amma might have been amused or puzzled that her daughter forgot a big kolam from that same morning but remembered every tangram piece.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at nine, a half-finished tangram kept pulling at her mind until she rushed back, while a finished kolam slipped from memory.

passage: Lokesh was four squares from finishing the number puzzle in his comic when the bus reached his stop. His brother Shankar tugged his sleeve. 'Get down, it's pouring!' They ran through the rain to the ration shop, where Amma had sent them for rice. The queue was long and loud. Lokesh stood holding the cloth bag, counting rows in his head. Seven in the corner, so the middle had to be... Shankar poked him. 'It's our turn, wake up!' Lokesh had forgotten to give the ration card. On the walk home, dripping, he kept muttering numbers. At home he didn't change his wet shirt. He opened the comic on the floor and filled the last four squares. 'Done!' Shankar held up yesterday's maze page. 'You finished this one too, remember?' Lokesh looked at it blankly. He didn't remember it at all.

qa.q: Where did Amma send Lokesh and Shankar?
qa.a: Amma sent them to the ration shop for rice.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh forget to give the ration card?
qa.a: His mind was stuck on the unfinished number puzzle, counting rows in his head, so he wasn't paying attention to the queue.

qa.q: What small step could Lokesh take next time he has to stop a puzzle suddenly?
qa.a: He could mark or quickly note where he stopped, so his mind can let go and focus on the errand.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt about Lokesh during the errand?
qa.a: Shankar was probably a little annoyed, having to poke him and handle the queue while Lokesh muttered numbers.

grounding: On a rainy errand a boy can't stop thinking about his unfinished number puzzle and rushes to complete it, while a finished maze slips from his memory.

passage:
When I was nine, beta, in our old house in Bhuj, my cousin Bhavna and I were doing a jigsaw of a peacock. Five hundred pieces. We had finished everything except the tail when my mother called me to the market.
All the way there and back I kept seeing that tail. Which blue piece went where? I bumped into a cow, I was so lost in it. My mother laughed at me.
My homework was finished that morning. I couldn't have told you one sum from it. But that tail, I remembered every gap.
I ran straight back, and Bhavna had waited. "Hansa, I didn't touch it," she said. We finished it together before dinner. Your Dadi has never forgotten that peacock.

qa.q: What picture was on the jigsaw?
qa.a: It was a jigsaw of a peacock.

qa.q: Why did young Hansa keep thinking about the tail at the market?
qa.a: She felt restless and a bit puzzled, because the unfinished tail stayed open in her mind while the finished homework slipped away.

qa.q: What was the choice inside the story that helped Hansa settle the nagging feeling?
qa.a: Rushing straight back and finishing the tail with Bhavna closed the open task, so her mind could rest.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt waiting without touching the puzzle?
qa.a: Bhavna probably felt loyal and a little impatient, wanting to finish it together and pleased when Hansa came running back.

grounding: A child called away mid-jigsaw keeps thinking about the unfinished part and rushes back, while her finished homework slips from mind.

passage:
Deepak had just four pieces left in the train jigsaw when the power went off and his sister Gopika called, "Come, we have to leave for Mama's wedding now!"
In the car, in the rain, Deepak couldn't stop thinking. The red engine piece. The corner with the smoke. Where did the last blue one go?
At the wedding, Gopika asked what he had eaten for breakfast. He didn't remember. He'd also finished his maths worksheet that morning and couldn't recall a single question. But he could picture every gap in the puzzle.
They got home late. The power was still off. Deepak took a torch, knelt on the floor and pressed the last four pieces in. Only then did he yawn.

qa.q: How many pieces did Deepak have left when the power went off?
qa.a: He had just four pieces left.

qa.q: How can you tell the unfinished jigsaw was on Deepak's mind?
qa.a: He felt restless and couldn't stop picturing the gaps, even at the wedding, and only relaxed enough to yawn once it was done.

qa.q: What could Deepak try next time he has to stop a puzzle suddenly?
qa.a: He could jot a quick note of what's left, like which pieces go where, so his mind can let it go until he returns.

qa.q: What is it like for Gopika to be with Deepak at the wedding?
qa.a: Gopika might find him distracted and a bit funny, since he can't remember breakfast but keeps thinking about a puzzle.

grounding: A child pulled away from a nearly finished jigsaw keeps thinking about it, forgets finished tasks and finishes it by torchlight.

passage:
On Sunday mornings Jaya did the newspaper word search in the flat's living room. She had found seven of the ten words when her cousin Devika called, "Jaya, come, we're late for the dentist!"
In the auto, Jaya muttered, "Pomegranate. Where's pomegranate?"
"You're still on that?" Devika laughed.
At the clinic, Devika asked what books Jaya had finished that week. Jaya frowned. She'd finished two, but couldn't remember the second one's name. Pomegranate, though. And the two words after it.
As soon as they got home, Jaya ran to the table, grabbed the pencil and circled the last three words. She let out a huge breath and flopped on the sofa, happy.

qa.q: How many of the ten words had Jaya found before leaving?
qa.a: She had found seven of the ten words.

qa.q: Why did Jaya let out a huge breath after circling the last words?
qa.a: She felt relieved and happy, because the unfinished word search had been tugging at her mind all morning.

qa.q: What could Jaya do the next time she is interrupted?
qa.a: She could write down the missing words on a slip so she doesn't have to keep them spinning in her head.

qa.q: How might Devika see Jaya muttering in the auto?
qa.a: Devika seems amused and a little puzzled that Jaya can't let go of the word search on the way to the dentist.

grounding: A child interrupted mid-word search keeps thinking about it and rushes back, while finished books slip from memory.

passage:
"Arohi, dinner. Now, please."
"Two more minutes, Maa. I'm on the sky part."
"The sky part will still be there after dinner."
"But it's all blue. I have to remember which blue goes where."
At the table: "Why are you staring at the wall?"
"I'm thinking about the corner piece, Maa. The one with half a cloud."
"Eat your dal. What did you do in school today?"
"I forgot. But I know the cloud piece is under the sofa cushion."
"Did you finish your maths homework?"
"I think so. I don't remember. Can I go now?"
Chandrika laughed. "Go. Finish it."
Arohi was back on the floor before her plate reached the sink.

passage:
Last Sunday, and I'm Deepak by the way, I was halfway through the thousand-piece train jigsaw with my cousin Charu when Papa said we had to go to Mausi's for lunch. I didn't want to go. The whole drive, I kept seeing the red engine with its missing wheel.
At Mausi's I lost at carrom twice because I was thinking about which piece fitted the wheel. Charu said I was "somewhere else". Funny thing: I can't remember what we ate there. But I remember exactly where the wheel piece was: near the box, face down.
When we got home, I ran to the table without taking off my shoes. It took four minutes. Then I felt calm, like a door had shut.

qa.q: Where was the wheel piece?
qa.a: Near the box, face down.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel once the jigsaw was finished?
qa.a: Deepak felt calm and relieved, like a door had shut, after a day of restless thinking.

qa.q: What could Deepak try next time before being called away?
qa.a: Note the next step, like where the wheel piece might go, so the open task nags less during lunch.

qa.q: How might Charu have seen Deepak at Mausi's?
qa.a: Charu saw Deepak as "somewhere else", distracted and losing at carrom, perhaps a bit amused or annoyed.

grounding: A child recalls being pulled away from an unfinished jigsaw, thinking of it all day, forgetting other things, and feeling calm only when it was done.

passage:
Classroom note, Grade 4. Kishore, maths teacher.
During activity period, Dhruv was halfway through the tangram puzzle when the bell rang for assembly. He left very slowly, looking back at the table. In assembly his lips were moving; I think he was still arranging triangles. Back in class he went straight to the puzzle before taking out his book, and finished the swan in two minutes. Interesting: when I asked about the song they had sung in assembly, he couldn't remember it at all.
Next time I'll give a two-minute warning before the bell and let children write down where they stopped. That may help them let go and listen.

qa.q: What shape did Dhruv finish?
qa.a: The swan.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling as he left for assembly?
qa.a: He felt reluctant and unsettled, his mind still pulled by the half-done tangram.

qa.q: How might the two-minute warning help?
qa.a: Children can write where they stopped, so the unfinished task nags less and they can focus on what comes next.

qa.q: How does the teacher see Dhruv's behaviour?
qa.a: Kishore finds it interesting that the unfinished puzzle held Dhruv's attention while the finished assembly song was forgotten.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child interrupted mid-puzzle thinking about it through assembly and rushing back to finish, while the finished event slips from memory.

passage:
Diwali cleaning day
I was halfway through my 300-piece jungle puzzle on the floor when Mummy called me to help clean the fans. I'm Yamini.
All through the cleaning, I kept thinking about the tiger's missing ear. Shankar asked me to pass the duster twice and I didn't hear him. I finished the curtains, then the shelves, and I don't even remember doing them.
The moment Mummy said, "Done!" I ran back to the puzzle. I found the tiger's ear in five minutes.
Funny thing: I've finished lots of puzzles and can't remember any of them. But this one I couldn't stop thinking about, just because it wasn't done.

qa.q: How many pieces was Yamini's puzzle?
qa.a: It was a 300-piece jungle puzzle.

qa.q: Why didn't Yamini hear Shankar ask for the duster?
qa.a: Yamini felt restless and distracted, still thinking about the unfinished puzzle.

qa.q: What could help Yamini focus on cleaning next time?
qa.a: Yamini could stop the puzzle at a clear point, or note the next piece to find, so it doesn't keep nagging.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel when Yamini doesn't hear?
qa.a: Shankar may feel a bit annoyed, having to ask twice while Yamini's mind is elsewhere.

grounding: Shows a child called away mid-puzzle during festival cleaning who keeps thinking about it and rushes back, while finished tasks slip away.

passage:
It was the summer holidays in the village, and Aditi was halfway through a wooden animal puzzle her Nani had bought at the fair. The elephant was missing its trunk.
Then Sangeeta, her cousin, called from the lane: "Aditi! The mangoes are ready, come pick!"
Aditi went. But under the mango tree, she kept thinking about the trunk. Where had that piece gone? Was it under the charpai? She dropped two mangoes.
"Aditi, what's wrong with you today?" Sangeeta laughed.
"The trunk!"
Aditi ran home before the basket was full. She found the piece under the charpai. Once the elephant was done, she forgot about it and went back to the mangoes.

qa.q: What piece was missing from the elephant?
qa.a: The elephant was missing its trunk.

qa.q: Why did Aditi drop two mangoes?
qa.a: She was restless and distracted, thinking about the unfinished puzzle.

qa.q: What could Aditi do next time she has to leave a puzzle?
qa.a: She could note where she thinks the missing piece is, so her mind can let go until she returns.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see Aditi running home?
qa.a: Sangeeta may be amused and puzzled, not knowing a missing trunk was nagging her cousin.

grounding: Shows a child called away from an unfinished puzzle who keeps thinking about it and rushes back, then forgets it once done.

passage:
It was the first night of Hanukkah in Haifa, and Noa was halfway through a jigsaw of the sea. Only the boat was left.
Her mother called, "Noa, candle time!" Noa went to the window with the family. She sang, but her eyes kept drifting to the table.
"Noa, where are you?" her cousin Olga whispered.
"The boat," Noa whispered back.
After the candles, everyone sat down to eat. Noa ate fast and slipped back to the puzzle. In ten minutes, the boat was done. She sighed happily.
The next day she couldn't remember what the finished puzzle looked like. But she remembered the boat that wasn't done.

qa.q: What part of the puzzle was left?
qa.a: Only the boat was left.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling as her eyes drifted to the table?
qa.a: She felt restless and pulled back to the unfinished puzzle.

qa.q: What could help Noa enjoy the candles without distraction next time?
qa.a: She could finish the puzzle earlier or tell herself exactly what's left, so it doesn't keep calling her.

qa.q: How might Olga feel when Noa whispers "The boat"?
qa.a: Olga may feel amused and a little puzzled by how much the puzzle holds Noa's mind.

grounding: Shows a child called away mid-puzzle during a festival who keeps thinking about it and rushes back to finish, while the finished puzzle soon slips from mind.

passage: During Holi week, the school library had a giant jigsaw of a tiger on the back table. Vinita was nearly done with the stripes when the bell rang for the colour-play assembly. "Come on!" Varun called. She went, but through all the gulal and music, she kept thinking about the empty corner by the tiger's ear. Where did that last curved piece go? She even dreamt of it. The spelling test she'd finished that morning? She couldn't remember a single word from it. The next day, she ran to the library before first bell, still with pink hands, and found the piece under the table. Snap. Done. By lunchtime, she'd forgotten all about the tiger.
